stories.title: Scion Group, Ares Acquire U.S. Student Housing Portfolio for $435M
stories.excerpt: In their second major acquisition this year, student housing owner and operator the Scion Group and private equity giant Ares Management have purchased a four-community student housing portfolio in Texas, Tennessee and Georgia for approximately $435 million. Scion and Ares bought the 2,316-bed portfolio from Schenk+, a real estate development and investment company led by Jared Schenk that specializes in off-campus student housing. Three of the communities that are part of the purchase were developed by Schenk+, while the fourth was acquired and repositioned by the firm, according to a Tuesday announcement from the buyers. The portfolio includes properties at the University of Georgia in Athens, the University of Tennessee in Knoxville and Texas State University in San Marcos. “Jared Schenk is one of the true pioneers of off-campus student housing, and he has built an incredible portfolio of high-quality communities,” Robert Bronstein, CEO of Scion, said in a statement. “This transaction provides a comprehensive exit for him and his investors. Scion is pleased to add another successful portfolio execution to our track record, and we are even more excited to welcome these communities to our portfolio.” Inland Real Estate Investment’s Nati Kiferbaum represented Schenk+ in the deal, while it was unclear whether Scion and Ares had any representation. Kiferbaum could not be reached for comment, while a spokesperson for Schenk+ did not immediately respond to a request for comment. News of the deal comes roughly three months after Scion and Ares completed the largest student housing portfolio deal so far in 2026. In late May, the joint venture acquired a 12-property student housing portfolio in the U.S. for $910 million from Harrison Street Asset Management (HSAM), as Commercial Observer previously reported. The portfolio included 7,578 beds across 10 states and 12 universities, including Arizona State University, Auburn University in Alabama and the University of Florida.
bullets: Scion Group + Ares acquire 2,316-bed student housing portfolio for $435M across Texas, Tennessee, Georgia
Properties at University of Georgia, University of Tennessee, Texas State University; second major deal for Scion/Ares in 2026
Off-campus student housing consolidation signals PE confidence in sector fundamentals and operator scale
stories.summary: Scion Group and Ares Management purchased a four-community, 2,316-bed student housing portfolio for approximately $435 million from Schenk+, acquiring properties near University of Georgia (Athens), University of Tennessee (Knoxville), and Texas State University (San Marcos). This marks the second major acquisition this year for the partnership. The deal reflects continued institutional investor appetite for off-campus student housing despite higher education headwinds.
stories.impact: Consolidation of student housing by well-capitalized PE players pressures smaller developers and operators in college towns. Limited supply elasticity around major state universities means Scion/Ares can raise rents and optimize NOI; signals confidence in student enrollment stability in these markets despite national demographic shifts. Worth monitoring occupancy and rate trends at comparable univ-adjacent properties in these three metros for demand signal confirmation.

stories.title: Logistics Property Lands Tenant for 217K-SF Houston-Area Warehouse
stories.excerpt: Logistics Property Company leased 217,758 square feet of build-to-suit warehouse space at CityPark Logistics Center, Building 7 in Missouri City, Texas, with Standex GRID / Amran Instrument Transformers (Standex GRID / Amran). Standex GRID / Amran will use the space as both a warehouse and manufacturing facility. CityPark Logistics Center is a 98-acre industrial park that includes five fully leased buildings totaling more than one million square feet. Construction on the new facility is underway, with an anticipated completion in Q2 2027. This new building will be Standex GRID / Amran’s largest North American location. CityPark Logistics Center was selected for its Southwest Houston location and its ability to accommodate a layout that meets Standex GRID/Amran’s office, production, and manufacturing needs. Cushman & Wakefield’s Beau Kaleel and Brooke Swerdlow assisted in the transaction. Standex GRID / Amran was represented by Steve King and Wesley King of CBRE. The general contractor is Burton Construction, with Powers Brown as the architect and Pape Dawson as the civil engineer.  The post Logistics Property Lands Tenant for 217K-SF Houston-Area Warehouse appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Standex GRID/Amran leases 217,758-sf build-to-suit warehouse at CityPark Logistics Center, Missouri City, Houston
Completion Q2 2027; largest North American facility for Standex; 98-acre park now >1M sf across five buildings

The facility, expected to complete in Q2 2027, will serve as Standex's largest North American location and support both warehouse and manufacturing operations. CityPark's 98-acre industrial park now totals over 1 million square feet across five fully leased buildings.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily. However, Standex's expansion into Southwest Houston (largest North American facility) suggests regional manufacturing/supply-chain activity; could drive downstream worker in-migration and rental demand if Standex hires significantly. Monitor labor demand and wage trends in Southwest Houston industrial corridor as leading indicator for multifamily renter job growth.

stories.title: 2026 World Cup Made Localized Impact on Retail, Dining in Host Cities
stories.excerpt: The bump in retail and dining visitations for the 11 U.S. host cities of the 2026 FIFA World Cup was localized, Colliers and Placer.ai say in a new report. Near the match venues, dining visits rose 53.7% and retail traffic rose 22% year-over–year, while gains across the larger metro areas were minimal. Sporting goods stores were the most consistent winner among retail categories during the 39-day tournament, according to 7 World Cup Lessons for Retail, Dining & Real Estate. Conversely, apparel stores and superstores experienced mixed results. Meanwhile, bars and pubs averaged a 9% increase in visits on match days. “Mega-events create enormous consumer demand, but proximity alone does not guarantee that businesses will capture it,” said Anjee Solanki, national director of retail services & practice groups | U.S. at Colliers. “The properties that performed best became part of the fan experience through the right tenant mix, gathering spaces, or activations. For landlords and retailers, the opportunity is to move beyond simply being near an event and create destinations that consumers actively choose to visit.” Pictured: MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, NJ, one of 11 U.S. venues for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The post 2026 World Cup Made Localized Impact on Retail, Dining in Host Cities appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 2026 World Cup retail/dining traffic up 53.7% near venues, only 22% retail traffic, minimal metro-wide gains
Sporting goods stores strongest performers; apparel stores, superstores mixed results; bars/pubs +9% on match days
Colliers/Placer.ai study: proximity alone insufficient; destination-quality tenant mix, activations, gathering spaces drove performance
stories.summary: Colliers and Placer.ai analysis of 2026 FIFA World Cup impact across 11 U.S. host cities found dining visits near match venues rose 53.7% year-over-year, while retail traffic rose 22%, but gains across broader metros were minimal. Sporting goods stores performed most consistently; bars/pubs averaged 9% gains on match days. Properties that succeeded created fan destination experiences through curated tenant mix, gathering spaces, and activations rather than relying on venue proximity alone.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development fundamentals. Brief event-driven retail/hospitality uplift in host metros does not materially shift residential demand or supply. However, the insight that destination-quality mixed-use activation drives traffic is relevant for developers planning live/work/retail communities (e.g., Woodrow House, Article 4): tenant curation and placemaking amenities outweigh raw location proximity for lease-up velocity and NOI.

stories.title: Woodfield Starts Deliveries of 325 Beltline Rental Units
stories.excerpt: Woodfield Development has begun residential deliveries at Woodrow House as the community’s first build-to-rent townhomes are completed along the Atlanta Beltline’s Westside Trail. It marks the opening phase of the 325-home mixed-income community and the beginning of residential occupancy. The venture will include apartments, build-to-rent units and live/work residences. The initial delivery includes 25 townhomes, representing the first homes available within Woodrow House. Additional townhomes and multifamily residences will continue delivering throughout the coming months, with the full community expected to open later this year. Located at 840 Woodrow St. SW, the development will include 12,000 square feet of neighborhood-serving retail. Amenities include a pool, fitness center, coworking spaces, pet amenities and landscaped gathering areas. Additional amenities, including the property’s podcast studio, club lounge and sky deck, will open as future phases of the community are completed. The post Woodfield Starts Deliveries of 325 Beltline Rental Units appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Woodfield Development opens first 25 build-to-rent townhomes at Woodrow House, Atlanta Beltline Westside Trail

stories.summary: Woodfield Development has begun initial deliveries at Woodrow House, a 325-unit mixed-income residential community along Atlanta's Beltline Westside Trail. The first phase includes 25 build-to-rent townhomes; additional townhomes and multifamily units will deliver throughout the year. The project includes 12,000 square feet of neighborhood-serving retail and amenities including a pool, fitness center, coworking spaces, a podcast studio, and a sky deck, with full opening targeted for late 2026.
stories.impact: Demonstrates strong Atlanta Beltline demand for mixed-income, experiential multifamily with retail/amenity activation. Early absorption signals and lease-up pace should be monitored; Beltline corridor is becoming a premium urban village pipeline. For TCR: indicator that Beltline submarkets (Westside, Eastside) can support higher-density, higher-amenity product with commanding rents; worth evaluating remaining Beltline developable sites for similar trophy mixed-use development in Atlanta.

stories.title: Jamestown Closes on Refis for Two Sandy Springs Retail Centers
stories.excerpt: Jamestown received a $72 million floating-rate loan from accounts managed by KKR to refinance Parkside Shops and Hammond Exchange in Sandy Springs. Cushman & Wakefield arranged the loan. The properties, which include more than more than 340,000 square feet of space, are on the corner of Roswell Road and Hammond Drive south of City Springs. Whole Foods anchors a long list of tenants, including Marshalls, HomeGoods, Petco, and The Springs Cinema & Taphouse. Jamestown paid a total of $93.85 million for the properties in 2018. The Atlanta Business Chronicle reports Jamestown has positioned the property for future mixed-use redevelopment opportunities. Cushman & Wakefield’s John Alascio was joined by Alex Hernandez, Alex Lapidus, Mitch Rothstein, Nick Scibelli and Mark Gilbert in representing Jamestown in the refinancing. Monitor for entitlement/redevelopment announcements; could signal nearby development opportunities and land value benchmarks for TCR Atlanta market analysis.

stories.title: Retail Location Intelligence Grows in Sophistication and Usage
stories.excerpt: In the late 1960s, science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke posited a now-famous law of the universe: “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” As the rapid advancement of technology, especially given the ongoing progress of artificial intelligence, often makes this seem truer by the day, its implications in commercial real estate are often of a type that would have seemed like pure voodoo to CRE professionals when Clarke put forth this statement. Here’s one example: A restaurant chain with over 3,500 locations in the U.S. is researching potential sites for additional stores in a certain part of Los Angeles. The chain has very specific parameters in mind, including a cash-on-cash return of at least 20 percent, at least $1.5 million in annual revenue, and a maximum cannibalization factor of the company’s other area stores of 10 percent. Punch this information into a computer program, press a button, and moments later the computer produces a detailed map of the neighborhood with a series of misshapen blobs representing the exact areas — down to specific streets and even addresses — where a new store would produce these results or better. In an ever-evolving boon for retailers, location intelligence has ascended to a level where platforms can predict retail success, including revenue and investment return figures, down to a specific site. These predictions are based on hundreds of demographic and psychographic factors as well as information such as competitive intelligence, complementary local businesses, local crime patterns, and the retailer in question’s own history. As one example, consultancy Bain & Company markets a location intelligence program called Vantage that evaluates current and prospective physical sites for retailers, driven by global data sets and machine learning analytics that translate its findings into a user-friendly location visualization dashboard. Technology enables data-driven site selection at scale, reducing manual underwriting, accelerating deployment
stories.summary: Advanced location intelligence platforms now combine AI, real-time data, and machine learning to enable hyper-granular site selection. A restaurant chain with 3,500+ U.S. locations can input specific parameters—20% cash-on-cash return, $1.5 million annual revenue, 10% maximum cannibalization—and receive maps pinpointing exact neighborhoods and addresses that meet criteria within moments, a process that would have taken weeks manually.
stories.impact: Indirect but significant for multifamily: competing retail/restaurant operators will deploy multifamily-adjacent sites more efficiently, reducing available corner/mixed-use parcels and raising land competition in high-velocity metros. Developers using similar tools for site selection can stay ahead. More important: retail co-tenants and site selection quality improve when anchors use AI; mixed-use projects with algorithmically-optimized retail tenants will lease faster and stabilize quicker, improving project IRR and refinance value.

stories.title: GreenBarn’s David Welsh and David Schonbraun Aren’t Afraid of a Little Complexity
stories.excerpt: A lot happened in the world in 2020: some bad, some ugly but also some good. Amid the tumult and upheaval came some new shoots — “green” ones, so to speak — and, a few years after that, a pairing of two industry veterans. David Welsh co-founded Normandy Real Estate Partners, an investment firm primarily focused on the Northeast, in 2002. After selling Normandy to Columbia Property Trust in 2019, he co-founded a new company, Senlac Ridge, with two of his Normandy partners in January 2020. David Schonbraun spent almost two decades at SL Green Realty as the office ownership giant’s chief investment officer, departing in 2021, before becoming Carlyle Group’s U.S. head of real estate credit. By 2023, Schonbraun opted for a different shade of green. Welsh bought out his two Senlac partners and rebranded the company to GreenBarn Investment Group, bringing in Schonbraun as his partner at the firm and Rithm Capital as a partner in its business. Three years later, GreenBarn has roughly $3.5 billion in investments under its belt and is carving out a niche for itself in a crowded market, one led by experience and the ability to tackle complex deals across sectors, as well as up and down the capital stack. If the GreenBarn name sounds familiar, you’ve likely heard about the firm’s myriad deals, from the restructuring of the $1.84 billion in debt on a Columbia Property Trust (CXP) office portfolio; to the recapitalization of 817 Broadway; to the $77 million mezzanine loan for Grubb Properties’ development at Manhattan’s 8 Carlisle Street; to the $112 million retail loan on Kushner Companies’ Monmouth Mall in New Jersey; to being awarded asset management duties at 20 Times Square. In short, its portfolio is anything but vanilla. “The hairier the deals, the better for us, because we feel very comfortable with complexity,” Schonbraun said during a July interview. “We’re happy operating where others shy away. stories.title: Butlr’s New Thermal Sensor Products Aim at Occupancy and Restrooms
stories.excerpt: Physical artificial intelligence technology company Butlr has launched two products — Ask Butlr and its Smart Cleaning module — for building operators. A Massachusetts Institute of Technology spinout, Butlr combines thermal body heat sensing technology and machine learning to infer human behavior without the use of cameras or other methods that compromise anonymity. Ask Butlr, an analyst AI tool that allows building operators to ask about occupancy and usage and get data-backed insights, is the Burlingham, Calif.-based company’s latest product. The Ask Butlr dashboard uses anonymized thermal sensor data that integrates with AI to provide insights on building occupancy, dwell time, foot traffic and energy consumption in the built environment. It also supports strategic space planning, operations and capital real estate investments with granular data gathered anonymously based on human behavior. That allows its physical AI and spatial intelligence platform to address current and future building needs. “We built Ask Butlr in response to the growing need among our customers for accurate first-party data and insights on buildings without compromising the privacy and anonymity of occupants,” Honghao Deng, CEO and co-founder of Butlr, said in an email. “This new offering quickly analyzes and presents information in an easy-to-understand format that empowers facilities managers, workplace decision-makers, and CRE professionals to optimize spaces while realizing stronger return on investment on their buildings.” The Smart Cleaning module, part of Butlr’s spatial intelligence platform, uses granular, anonymized usage data to reduce restroom cleaning costs. Butlr’s wall- or ceiling-mounted thermal sensors are placed outside a restroom to capture foot traffic and occupancy data. The Smart Cleaning module provides a deeper level of insight based on bathroom door swings. Inside the restroom, an optional touch module enables facilities staff to confirm cleanings are complete. stories.title: Forbearances, Modifications Carry Weight in Latest Data
stories.excerpt: CRED iQ tracked 82 modified commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) and commercial real estate collateralized loan obligation (CRE CLO) loans with a combined $2.36 billion in outstanding balance from May through July 2026. The mix looks different than it did a few quarters ago as “extend and pretend” hasn’t disappeared, but it’s no longer the whole story. Forbearances and combination modifications are now carrying meaningful weight alongside straight maturity extensions, and the balance is concentrated in midsize loans rather than mega-loans. The property type with the most modifying isn’t hotels or office anymore — it’s multifamily. Of the $2.36 billion modified during the period, maturity date extensions remained the single largest category: 21 loans totaling $802.5 million, or 34 percent of modified balance (25.6 percent of the loan count). Forbearances followed at 15 loans and $514 million (21.8 percent of balance), while combination modifications — deals pairing an extension with other relief, such as a paydown, rate adjustment or reserve requirement — accounted for 10 loans and $345.6 million (14.7 percent of balance). Of the remaining 36 loans, $695.4 million (29.5 percent of balance) fell into other or miscellaneous modification categories. Taken together, extensions, forbearances and combination mods — the categories most closely associated with lenders buying time on distressed collateral — made up 70.5 percent of modified balance this period, down from the near-universal “extend and pretend” theme of recent reports. Lenders appear to be reaching for a broader tool kit than a simple maturity push. Multifamily loans led modification activity by a wide margin, a shift from the hotel- and office-driven distress of previous quarters: Multifamily: 35 loans totaling $1.14 billion (48.4 percent of modified balance) Hotel: 15 loans totaling $493.8 million (20.9 percent) Retail: Six loans totaling $236.7 million (10 percent) Office: 17 loans totaling $226.2 mi
bullets: CRED iQ tracks $2.36B modified CMBS/CRE CLO loans (May–July 2026); multifamily now leading property type for modifications
34% maturity extensions ($802.5M, 21 loans), 21.8% forbearances ($514M, 15 loans), 14.7% combo mods ($345.6M, 10 loans)
Shift from 'extend and pretend' mega-loans to meaningful forbearances + combo mods in midsize deals; indicates refinance stress in sector
stories.summary: CRED iQ data from May–July 2026 tracks $2.36 billion in modified CMBS and CRE CLO loans. Multifamily has become the property type with the highest modification volume, surpassing hotels and office. Modifications break down as: 34% maturity extensions ($802.5M), 21.8% forbearances ($514M), and 14.7% combination modifications ($345.6M), concentrated in midsize loans. The balance reflects a shift from simple 'extend and pretend' strategies to more diverse relief structures.
stories.impact: Critical signal for multifamily underwriting and capital strategy: multifamily loan modifications exceeding office/hotel signals sector-wide refinance stress, likely driven by higher cap rate assumptions, higher leverage expectations, and rate-lock pressure on 2020–2021 vintage deals. For TCR acquisitions: tightened debt structures, higher equity equity requirements, and longer stabilization timelines are now standard. Conversely, distressed multifamily asset sales (from modification defaults) may create opportunistic acquisition windows in select metros; monitor CRED iQ and RealPage data for cap rate compression and spread widening.

stories.title: Terra Lands $245M Financing for Newly Completed Upland Park Development
stories.excerpt: Terra secured $245 million in permanent financing for the newly completed first phase of Upland Park, a $1 billion, 47-acre mixed-use transit-oriented development in West Miami-Dade County. Slate Property Group provided the financing following the completion of the 578-unit multifamily community, which is already more than 60% leased in less than 90 days since opening earlier this summer. Construction of the project’s second residential phase, which will add another 484 multifamily apartments, is expected to begin later this year. Located at 1455 NW 121st Avenue, Upland Park’s first residential phase features a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom residences with select den layouts, ranging from approximately 700 to 1,528 square feet. Monthly rental rates start in the $2,000s. The project is designed by PPK Architects, in collaboration with master plan architect Arquitectonica. Community amenities include a pool and separate children’s pool, clubhouse, pickleball courts, outdoor grilling and gathering areas, playground, dog park, game lawn and landscaped green spaces overlooking the community lake. The post Terra Lands $245M Financing for Newly Completed Upland Park Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Terra secures $245M permanent financing (Slate Property Group) for 578-unit first phase, Upland Park, West Miami-Dade

stories.summary: Terra closed $245 million in permanent financing from Slate Property Group for the newly completed first phase of Upland Park, a 578-unit multifamily community in West Miami-Dade County. The property has achieved over 60% occupancy in less than 90 days since opening, with rents starting at $2,000 and ranging to $1,500+ for mixed unit types. Upland Park is a $1 billion, 47-acre transit-oriented development; construction of a second 484-unit residential phase is expected to begin later in 2026.
stories.impact: Strong demand signal for West Miami-Dade TOD multifamily: 60%+ pre-lease and rapid lease-up post-opening indicate sustained rental demand and rent growth potential in Miami submarket despite Florida's competitive multifamily supply pipeline. For TCR: validates premium pricing and amenity investment strategy in transit-accessible, mixed-use Miami submarkets (Wynwood, Allapattah, Little Haiti corridors). Rents at $2K+ suggest renter willingness to pay for location + experience; monitor Upland Park stabilized occupancy and year-2 rent growth as comp for similar West/Central Miami projects in underwriting.
